output.headline: Police act on livestreamed footage to hold far-right activist Daniel Thomas over Channel dinghy
output.bodyHtml:
Police have arrested the far-right agitator and anti-migrant activist Daniel Thomas on suspicion of “criminal damage with intent to endanger life”, after he filmed himself appearing to slash the side of a dinghy in the middle of the Channel, while a rescuer was onboard.

Hampshire and Isle of Wight constabulary said a 37-year-old man, of no fixed abode, had been arrested after a boat that had an emergency responder onboard was damaged in the Channel. The man was arrested “on suspicion of destroying ships or fixed platforms or endangering their safety”.

Police said he remained in custody on Thursday. He was also suspected of committing “criminal damage, criminal damage with intent to endanger life, and conduct endangering ships, structures or individuals”.

Thomas apparently managed to film and upload footage of his own arrest before police were able to stop him. On Wednesday night a 56-second clip was uploaded to his YouTube platform showing a police officer telling him that he was being arrested on suspicion of criminal damage “recklessly endangering someone’s life”.

Thomas said: “I understand. I knew this was coming.”

Asylum seekers had been helped to safety before the incident. The force had earlier said that it was looking at footage livestreamed by Thomas, in which he can reportedly be seen using a knife to stab and slash an inflatable dinghy in the middle of the Channel after the asylum seekers had been helped to safety, but with a French rescue worker who had just got onboard.

His footage shows the rescue worker climbing back on the larger boat after Thomas’s boat sped away. Thomas’s footage appeared to show him approaching one of dinghies, which was empty, shouting: “Let’s get rid of that boat.” After the rescue worker got onboard, Thomas shouted: “Get off the boat. You’ve got time to get off the boat.”

Thomas, who goes by the name Danny Tommo, had spent the afternoon in a boat, filming himself as he tracked two dinghies carrying asylum seekers from France to the UK. The livestreamed footage was watched by more than 200,000 people.

A longtime associate of fellow far-right activist Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, AKA Tommy Robinson, Thomas this summer gathered dozens of nationalist protest groups under the umbrella anti-immigration movement Patriot Platform. The organisation was behind marches this month in Dover and Portsmouth, when masked men in black gathered and protested over immigration and asylum policy. Thomas repeatedly told his followers they should march silently, without violence and avoid doing anything that could lead to arrests.

Most small boats carrying asylum seekers across to the UK are escorted to shore by rescue services or Border Force vessels, and no unescorted small boats had been recorded since 6 September 2025. His arrest came amid renewed focus on the Home Office’s handling of small-boat arrivals in the UK, after there were two uncontrolled landings from the Channel in two days.

The home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, has ordered an urgent review by Border Security Command, describing the failure to intercept the two boats as “not acceptable”.

The education secretary, Lucy Powell, said: “You can’t stop everything all of the time”, after 21 people were detained when a boat evaded Border Force to reach the beach of Samphire Hoe in Dover on Wednesday. Another dinghy made an uncontrolled landing in Folkestone on Monday morning.

Speaking on BBC Radio 4’s Today programme, Powell said: “Of course, it’s a concern. That’s why the home secretary has demanded and ordered this urgent review, because this is not what we want to see. This is not acceptable.”
output.standfirst: The 37-year-old is in custody on suspicion of crimes including criminal damage with intent to endanger life, after footage appeared to show him slashing a dinghy with a French rescue worker onboard

output.headline: Andy Burnham begins to win progressives back to Labour, and tactical voting could put a majority within touching distance, poll finds
output.bodyHtml:
Labour could come within touching distance of a majority, with progressive voters pushing Reform UK into fourth place, if tactical voting is widespread at the next election, a major poll has found.

Andy Burnham is beginning to attract a significant number of left-leaning voters back to Labour, motivated by a desire to stop Nigel Farage, the results suggest.

Twice as many voters have returned to Labour from the left as from the right since April.

The poll of more than 8,000 voters, shared with the Guardian, suggests a widespread openness to voting tactically. It also shows the prime minister’s most successful electoral strategy would be to unite the centre and left bloc of voters, while the right remains split.

It would be a marked contrast to the tactics of Keir Starmer’s Labour before the 2024 general election, when the party tried to attract more conservative older voters. Such a tactic would be likely to unsettle some in Labour, given the same strategy was deployed for Ed Miliband’s failed bid in 2015, albeit before Reform’s arrival as a major electoral force.

Related: From idealists to struggling sceptics: how Labour’s majority depends on five progressive voter types – in charts

The poll on the eve of Labour’s annual conference in Liverpool shows a significant shift of left-leaning voters towards Burnham’s Labour and will encourage those in the party who are thinking of gambling on an early election while Reform’s ratings are ebbing and while leftwing parties such as the Greens appear to be losing momentum.

The previously unreleased research, including a seat-by-seat MRP model, was conducted by Survation and the progressive activist site 38 Degrees in Burnham’s first month as prime minister.

It suggests Labour would be the largest party in parliament if an election took place today, on 272 seats, a four-point lead. This would mean achieving 42% of parliamentary seats with 28% of the vote.

Reform would become the official opposition on 153. This represents 24% of seats – the same as its vote share. The Conservatives would fall to third place with 85.

Two hundred seats are tight marginals decided by under five points, meaning a two- to three-point swing could move about 100 seats that are likely to decide a future election. But in a sign of the volatility of the polls, a far higher percentage of voters are open to tactical voting in those seats when they cite their preferred party.

If voters are prepared to switch to one of the two frontrunners in their seats, rather than their preferred party, then Reform UK’s seat count would fall dramatically, favouring Labour and the Conservatives.

About 18% of voters who live in a seat where tactical voting would make a substantial difference say they are willing to do so but are not yet doing so. If those voters decided to vote tactically, Reform UK would be reduced to 62 seats, giving Labour 319 – six short of a majority.

Of the 91 seats where Reform would cease to be the most likely winner, 46 would go to the Conservatives and 43 to Labour. The projection is unlikely to be exact at this stage in the electoral cycle.

In 59 seats, Reform’s chances of winning fell by more than 50 points. Among these are the Wrekin, Torridge and Tavistock, and North West Cambridgeshire – all of which have Reform as the most likely leader under the “normal” assumptions but lose out to the Conservatives under a scenario with more tactical voting.

In 2024, the now-chancellor, John Healey, held Rawmarsh and Conisbrough with 49% of the vote, with Reform in second place on 28.6%. If tactical voting increases, the MRP gives Labour a 76% chance of holding the seat in this scenario; its base modelling indicates that Reform could win a tight race in the seat, with a 51% chance, which plummets under the tactical scenario.

In Bassetlaw, Reform could lose even as its own vote share rises from 35% to 40%, because tactical voting would lift Labour further – from 32% to 40%. The Conservatives, Liberal Democrats and Greens would lose supporters if this switching took place. The forecast estimates that the winner would shift from Reform, with a 77% chance, to Labour, with a 58% chance.

Newark, held by the Conservative-turned-Reform MP Robert Jenrick, is forecast to flip to the Conservatives under both scenarios, although under heavier tactical voting the chance of a Conservative win increases from 68% to more than 99% should Labour backers vote Conservative to stop him.

Damian Lyons Lowe, Survation’s chief executive, said: “Estimating tactical voting is a complex consideration, but the mechanics here are simple. Four in 10 voters are currently backing a party that can’t finish in the top two where they live and are willing to vote tactically.

“But when we ask whether they would lend their vote to the stronger local contender in a two-horse race, around half said yes. That gap – worth some 18 points of the national electorate – is an enormous untapped reservoir for parties looking to squeeze voters.

“Should these voters act as they say, our model shows Reform falling from second place to fourth, losing around 90 seats, despite its own vote share actually going up. Reform-leaning Conservatives will consolidate too. Reform doesn’t collapse; it risks being outnumbered, seat by seat, by voters coordinating around whoever is best placed locally on the left and right.”

The prediction is also complicated by the sheer number of seats Labour won in 2024 from the Conservatives where the party has been polling as low as third over the past year. Progressive voters living in seats such as Labour-held Southend would be unlikely to opt to vote for the Conservatives, even if they were technically the best placed to beat Reform at the next election, showing the limitations of predictions around tactical voting.

The poll also suggests Labour is winning considerable numbers of voters back from other leftwing parties, though not from Reform. The share of Labour’s lost 2024 voters going to the Greens, Liberal Democrats, Plaid Cymru or the Scottish National party has fallen from 60% to 46%; but on the right, of those lost to Reform or the Tories, it has fallen from 27% to 24%.

Veronica Hawking, the campaigns director at 38 Degrees, said the polling indicated a far more optimistic public mood than before the Labour conference last year, but there was also significant expectation that Burnham needed to deliver.

“There are signs of optimism and even hope, but what has not changed is the way voters are crying out for bold action, fast,” she said. “The results show a huge amount of common ground between voters, especially when it comes to the cost of living. Voters who have moved in different directions since the general election two years ago are united by the fact that action on the cost of living crisis will have the single biggest bearing on their future vote.”
output.standfirst:
Progressives are motivated by desire to stop Nigel Farage, polling suggests; widespread tactical voting could push Reform into fourth place, though Labour would still be six seats short of a majority

output.headline: Rail industry steps up protection for staff with more CCTV, body cameras and better reporting
output.bodyHtml:
Improved reporting processes and more CCTV and body-worn cameras for frontline staff are among the factors the rail industry says lie behind a record high of almost 25,000 reported assaults on Great Britain’s railways in a year.

A spokesperson for Network Rail and train operators said: “Violence, abuse and intimidation directed at passengers or staff are completely unacceptable. The rail industry works closely with British Transport Police to investigate incidents, support victims and bring offenders to justice.”

They said the numbers also reflected greater intelligence sharing, improved reporting processes, and more CCTV and body-worn cameras for frontline staff.

The chief inspector of railways at the Office of Rail and Road (ORR), Richard Hines, said: “The increase in reported assaults is concerning. No one on the railway should be subjected to violence, threats or abuse.

“We’re working with industry and our trade union colleagues to address work-related violence and harassment, including through recent guidance which sets out what we expect from rail employers.

“This includes understanding where the risks are, putting effective controls in place, encouraging staff to report incidents and providing appropriate support afterwards. Our inspectors will continue to check how these risks are being managed.”

On the London Underground, where there is single counting, the number of assaults on the workforce fell slightly last year. The ORR report noted that the headline numbers of reported assaults can include multiple counts in a single incident, for example for both harassment and common assault, while workforce assaults are now recorded even if no physical injury occurs.

The chief executive of the Rail Safety and Standards Board, Mark Phillips, said the rail industry was taking action to better protect staff, but the figures “underline the need for a change in public behaviour and greater respect for the people who keep the railway running safely every day”.

The figures partly reflect increased reporting and zero-tolerance campaigns on public transport, but also underline concerns flagged by unions about the ongoing threats to frontline workers as well as passengers, and the availability of transport police.

Unions said the “horrendous” figures showed the need for more staff and policing, as the ORR revealed a sharp increase in assaults on the travelling public and on railway staff last year.

There were 13,464 reported assaults against passengers and members of the public on the mainline railway in 2025-26, up 36% on the previous year and the highest number recorded by the ORR since it started tracking the figures in 2004.

Assaults on rail staff were up 12% in a year to 11,289 reported incidents, mainly verbal abuse but including nearly 2,500 physical assaults – an average of about seven every day.

The assaults on members of the public included startling rises in cases of harassment, up 52% year on year, and common assault, up by 30%.

The RMT general secretary, Eddie Dempsey, said the numbers were horrendous but chimed with the union’s own surveys showing two-thirds of its members had experienced some form of violence at work in the past year.

He said: “We are calling for a significant increase in staffing across public transport, including an end to lone working. We also clearly need stronger legal protections for public transport workers against assaults at work.

“British Transport Police funding cuts have also been disastrous which has undermined a proper policing presence on all public transport.”

Reports in recent years have highlighted that women and girls were at particular risk, while the growing number of assaults year on year since the pandemic has coincided with pressure on British Transport Police numbers.

The abuse and intimidation faced by frontline staff on the railways has also been seen in sectors including retail and in the NHS. The British Retail Consortium warned over “endemic” violence towards shop workers earlier this year, while the number of reports of violence against NHS staff by patients surpassed 100,000 in 2025.

The Department for Transport and British Transport Police were approached for comment.
output.standfirst:
Improved reporting and zero-tolerance campaigns partly explain a record high of almost 25,000 reported assaults on rail workers and the public, which unions say shows the need for more staff and policing

output.headline: High oil prices have had less impact on other prices than the Bank of England worried, says its chief economist
output.bodyHtml:
High oil prices have had less impact on other prices across the economy than the Bank of England had feared, its chief economist said on Thursday, as a global sell-off in government bonds put fresh upward pressure on UK borrowing costs before a tough budget for John Healey next month.

The yield – effectively the interest rate – on 10-year UK bonds, known as gilts, had risen to 5.38 per cent by mid-morning on Thursday, approaching the 19-year high set last week.

Higher interest rates raise the upfront cost of government investment and feed through into Office for Budget Responsibility forecasts of whether the chancellor is on course to meet Labour’s fiscal rules.

Analysts believe recent increases in yields have wiped out more than half of the £24bn “headroom” against the rules that the former chancellor Rachel Reeves had built up at the time of the spring statement in March.

Related: The perilous economic conditions facing the UK can be traced back to Trump | Richard Partington

Healey, her successor, has repeatedly promised to meet Labour’s fiscal rules with a “buffer against uncertainty”, though it is widely expected to be significantly lower than £24bn.

Treasury sources insist the budget will be “focused”, with important spending decisions postponed to a review next year; rebuilding the buffer to £24bn would be likely to require large tax increases or spending cuts.

Investors across the main markets have been ditching bonds in recent weeks in a wave of selling prompted by fears of higher inflation and interest rates as the conflict in the Middle East rumbles on.

The Bank of England chief economist, Clare Lombardelli, stressed that high oil prices had had less impact on other prices across the economy than the Bank had feared; but the longer they remained high, the greater the risk of inflation becoming entrenched.

In a speech on Thursday, she said the longer oil prices remained elevated as a result of the war, the more likely it was that UK interest rates would have to rise.

“The longer higher energy prices persist, the greater the risk that indirect effects build and that inflation expectations, wage bargaining and price-setting behaviour begin to adjust in response,” she told an economic conference in Warsaw, Poland.

“On that basis, policy is increasingly likely to need to tighten if elevated energy prices persist, absent clear evidence of disinflation or weaker activity.”

Lombardelli’s message echoed that of the Bank governor, Andrew Bailey, after the nine-member monetary policy committee left interest rates on hold at 3.75 per cent last week.

Andy Burnham’s government has promised to offer consumers a “breathing space” against the rising cost of living, at a time when higher rates would mean increased mortgage costs for homeowners.

The Bank is also expecting an eye-watering 24 per cent rise in the quarterly energy price cap that determines household utility bills in January, if oil prices remain high.

As the bond sell-off continued to worsen on Thursday, yields on 30-year US Treasury bonds surged to 5.444 per cent – the highest level since 2004.

Alongside higher inflation, investors appear to be concerned about the risks of uncontrolled US government spending. Some analysts also suggest large-scale bond issuance by AI firms is undermining demand for treasuries.
output.standfirst:
Clare Lombardelli says the effect has been smaller than the Bank had feared, but higher rates grow more likely the longer energy prices stay high, as a global bond sell-off lifts 10-year gilt yields to 5.38 per cent, near a 19-year high, narrowing Healey’s room for manoeuvre

output.headline: Scholars and conservationists hold Newcastle University to account over Anant Ambani sustainability professorship
output.bodyHtml:
Scholars and conservationists are holding Newcastle University to account after it appointed the heir to an Indian oil and gas fortune who runs a controversial mega-zoo as a professor of sustainability, and the university is facing a backlash.

Academic staff and Indian and international conservationists and environmentalists met the university’s announcement with incredulity and derision.

Ramachandra Guha, a leading Indian public intellectual and the author of the book Speaking With Nature: The Origins of Indian Environmentalism, said: “I must say that it is a rather mystifying choice. As a scholar of Indian and global environmentalism, I can name at least 50 – perhaps 100 – individuals who are far better qualified to be thus honoured. They include soil scientists, energy scientists, water conservation experts, community forest workers, ecologists, pollution abatement experts etc who have made real and tangible contributions to a more sustainable future for India and Indians.

“I wonder on whose advice Newcastle University has acted, and whether it did due diligence on what has and has not been done in these fields. Its appointment of Mr Ambani is puzzling in the extreme, and is likely to adversely affect the university’s institutional credibility and intellectual standing.”

Bhuvan Mangalore, an Indian investigator into illegal wildlife trade who is completing a dissertation on Vantara at Anglia Ruskin University, asked: “Is this a joke?”

Prof Matt Perry, the chair of the University and College Union branch at Newcastle University, said staff members had objected to the appointment citing environmental concerns.

Prof Lyla Mehta, the head of the climate, environment and sustainability department at the University of Sussex’s Institute of Development Studies, shared concerns that “as public funding for universities falls, there is a real danger that billionaire and corporate money begins to shape academia”.

She said: “Universities are supposed to be places that question power and hold corporations to account, not give them academic legitimacy.”

Lorne Stockman, a research co-director at Oil Change International, said: “At a time when the climate crisis demands an urgent phaseout of oil and gas, we must demand our publicly funded institutions do better.”

The university announced that Anant Ambani had been given a professorship of practice for “his work in conservation, biodiversity protection, animal welfare and environmental stewardship” and “significant contributions to advancing a more sustainable future”.

A Newcastle University spokesperson said: “The award of a professorship of practice recognises Mr Ambani’s contributions to conservation, biodiversity protection, animal welfare and environmental stewardship through his work with Vantara, a wildlife rescue and conservation initiative, and as the executive lead for the Reliance Group’s transition toward a green energy future.”

Ambani is the son of India’s richest person, Mukesh Ambani, who made his fortune primarily in oil and gas, owns the world’s largest oil refinery and has close ties with the ruling Bharatiya Janata party (BJP). Mukesh Ambani has enthusiastically praised BJP policies, and firms linked to his Reliance conglomerate have recently made significant donations to the party. The prime minister, Narendra Modi, attended Anant Ambani’s lavish 2024 wedding in Mumbai.

Anant Ambani, 31, who leads on renewable energy on the Reliance Group’s executive board and is worth an estimated £90bn, has set up Vantara, a 1,400-hectare (3,500-acre) private zoo near the family’s oil refining facilities in Gujarat, which reportedly has more than 150,000 animals including 200 lions, 250 leopards and 900 crocodiles, and where he hosted his opulent pre-wedding celebrations attended by celebrity guests and politicians.

Vantara has never been found guilty of any wrongdoing. Conservation groups have previously raised questions about how some of the animals were sourced, given many were endangered species.

In April, Anant Ambani launched Vantara University, billed as the world’s first global university dedicated to wildlife conservation and veterinary science.

In 2025, an investigation by the German newspaper Süddeutsche Zeitung found that many animals delivered to Vantara arrived through countries with opaque wildlife trading networks such as the Democratic Republic of the Congo and the United Arab Emirates, raising concerns that endangered species may have been illegally trafficked.

In August last year, India’s supreme court cleared the zoo’s operators of any wrongdoing, in an investigation which lasted less than three weeks. A subsequent fact-finding mission into the zoo by Cites, the UN body that regulates the trade of endangered species, found that some of the permits used to bring animals to Vantara were probably forged.

Its report said: “There is a need for caution to ensure that imports of large numbers of animals by these facilities are not inadvertently creating a demand for illegally sourced animals.”

Cites recommended restrictions on India’s imports of endangered wild animals. However, it subsequently reversed its decision after objections from India, the US and Japan at a Cites meeting after they argued there was not enough proof of illegal imports.

In August, the zoo launched a “reset” in its operations, appointing a former Cites head to oversee its operations, and said it would voluntarily pause all wildlife imports until June next year.

Vantara has declined to comment. The Ambani family and Vantara have previously denied the allegations of wildlife trafficking. They have said: “Our mission and focus continues to be the rescue, rehabilitation and care of animals.”
output.standfirst: Ramachandra Guha names soil scientists, ecologists and community forest workers as better qualified, while the role for oil heir Anant Ambani, son of India’s richest person, who runs a controversial mega-zoo, meets backlash and incredulity

output.headline: US and China extend Busan trade truce to 10 January as Trump welcomes Xi on the tarmac
output.bodyHtml:
The world’s two biggest economies have agreed to extend their temporary trade truce, with Scott ⁠Bessent, the US treasury secretary, announcing that the US ⁠and ​China agreed on Wednesday to extend the so-called Busan ⁠agreement.

Bessent, who met the Chinese ‌vice-premier He Lifeng earlier on Wednesday, told Fox News the agreement would be extended until 10 January, two months after it was due to expire.

Donald Trump has welcomed Xi Jinping to the US in person, taking the unusual step of greeting the Chinese leader on the tarmac at Joint Base Andrews to kick off his state visit to Washington.

Related: AI looms large over Trump-Xi meeting amid deep distrust between US and China

A lavish arrival ceremony met Xi’s plane, with a 30-metre-long (100ft) red carpet flanked by US service members, a military flyover by two B-1 bombers and a presentation of the flags and national anthems of both countries.

Trump and the first lady, Melania, travelled to the military base in Maryland, just outside Washington, on Wednesday evening to personally shake hands with Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan – a step beyond the usual practice of US presidents, who typically welcome foreign leaders at the White House.

More pageantry will follow, with a formal state welcome on the South Lawn of the White House, private tea with the US president and first lady, and a tour of the National Archives, among other special events.

Xi’s visit is expected to be filled with ceremonial displays that reciprocate the treatment Trump received when he visited China earlier this year.

By greeting the Chinese leader at his plane, rather than at the White House, Trump shows how far he is willing to go to honour Xi.

“He’s coming on our soil,” Melania Trump said of the visit to Fox & Friends on Wednesday morning, “and we need to welcome them with the most respect.”

The White House has invited major tech leaders, such as executives from OpenAI, Apple, xAI, Microsoft, Nvidia, Meta and others, to a state dinner being held for Xi on Thursday.

Over the two-day visit, Trump and Xi must confront many thorny issues, including the simmering trade war, the race in artificial intelligence development and geopolitical instability.

The US and China have long been competing to develop increasingly powerful technology, but the race to further AI has become a major topic among tech companies – especially after several executives came forward to warn about the dangers of rapid development.

Trump has promoted more investment in the technology so the US can beat China in the race, and has dismissed concerns that AI development could harm people.

“There is a SICK conspiracy going on against AI and Data Centers, and the only one that is happy about it is China. WHOEVER WINS AI, WINS! We are leading China, and all others, and will continue to do so,” Trump wrote on Truth Social last week.

The president and members of the administration have insisted that leading AI development also means leading the world militarily and economically – further raising the stakes for the US and China.

Xi’s visit comes as world leaders gather in New York for the United Nations general assembly, although the Chinese leader will not address the meeting. He has attended the UNGA just once since becoming president in 2012.

“It’s pretty notable that Xi Jinping is ⁠coming to Washington in the same week as the general assembly, but does not feel bothered to come up to New York,” Richard Gowan of the International Crisis Group told Reuters. “I think a lot of people will say: ‘Where is the real center of decision-making?’”

The carefully orchestrated arrival ceremony had one discordant note, when Trump visibly winced at the sound of a US military jet flying overhead as he stood alongside Xi on the red carpet, listening to the US national anthem. Video of the moment showed that while Trump recoiled from the sound of the flyover, Xi remained impassive, as did the wives of both men.

The moment, which was widely mocked online, was captured on a White House livestream but was not included in the edited highlights of the ceremony that Trump’s aides released later.

Robert Mackey contributed reporting
output.standfirst:
Treasury secretary announces extension of the ‘Busan agreement’ pausing trade war hostilities until 10 January as president lays out red carpet, with the AI race among thorny issues the leaders must confront

  • AI, trade, Taiwan and climate: what will and won’t be on agenda at Trump-Xi summit
